doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Learning repertoire and Ellis Marsalis's trick tunes
summary: Bassists cannot fake tunes; Caine recalls Ellis Marsalis calling unknown tunes at Snug Harbor and the need to accept public humiliation.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Personally I think the bass player is often times the most important cog in the machine, and I feel like there’s a lot of — not pressure, but a bass player has to know the tunes. Horn players — I’m a horn player, and you can fake it. You can half know a tune and you can half play the melody and make it like this is my interpretation. Right?

And if you’re hearing the changes you usually can make your way through the thing and not be too embarrassed. But how do you, as a bassist, how have you and how do you get a repertoire of tunes in your memory?

It’s hard. I mean other things that advantage horn players and guitar players have is that you know you can fake your way through the melody and then wait for the other guy to solo, and you can hear it. But yeah, beat one I have to do something. It’s hard I mean there’s a thousand, a million tunes and I don’t know them all and even tunes you know, people play them differently. One of my great experiences was playing with Ellis Marsalis when I was in New Orleans and starting out, because I used to do his trio gig every week at Snug, and he would inevitably call a tune he knew you didn’t know. And he’d kind of go through it rubato, kind of modern, like some standard. And then he’d just kind of look at you and he’d kind of laugh, ‘cause he knew you didn’t know it. And he’d go three-four and then you just had to hear your way through it.
Could you stand on the side of the piano so you could see his left hand when possible?

Yeah but at Snug Harbor you couldn’t ‘cause you were on the other side. I mean I’ve always just tried to be honest. I mean you hear it and if you can’t you drop out or listen or you know, and just wait for your ears to develop. I mean once you accept public humiliation it’s like it’s pretty easy from there. That’s key. You’ve got to do that.
Once — I want to make sure I got that. Once you accept public humiliation.
Yeah Once you’re okay with being made to look like an idiot in front of thousands of people, it’s all downhill from there.
Well yeah, exactly. Depending how you look at it.
